question: The Commission’s proposal to set up an instrument for agile and rapid defence innovation (the ‘AGILE’ programme) is an important step in fast-tracking civil and dual-use technologies into defence applications and bolstering the EU’s defence innovation ecosystem.

In light of Russia’s continued war of aggression against Ukraine, the urgent need to scale up Europe’s defence industrial capabilities and intensifying technological competition, the rapid operational deployment of disruptive technologies is crucial for Europe’s security and technological sovereignty. At the same time, the proposal currently contains very few provisions on the future of the instrument beyond 2027.

Notably absent are a review clause, reporting requirements, a requirement to design a follow‑up instrument and indications as to how successful AGILE mechanisms are to be integrated into future defence instruments. 1.
How does the Commission plan to assess the strategic impact of AGILE, particularly with regard to strengthening the EU’s defence innovation ecosystem?
Does the Commission intend to set up a formal review mechanism or a roadmap to continue or extend AGILE beyond 2027?
How are the lessons learned from AGILE to be taken into account in future EU defence instruments such as the EDF, EUDIS or successor programmes?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.8.2026) The proposal for a Regulation establishing the Programme for Agile and Rapid Defence Innovation (AGILE)1 includes clear reporting obligations in line with the Commission’s Better Regulation2 requirements.

The explanatory memorandum and the legislative financial and digital statement accompanying the proposal provides for an implementation report and sets out several performance indicators which will support the assessment of AGILE’s results. The Commission recalls that the AGILE programme is designed to be implemented within the current Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF)3.
As such, the proposal cannot contain provisions concerning the future of the instrument beyond 2027, which would prejudge discussions in the context of the next MFF.

At the same time, the Commission has sought to ensure a legal framework in its proposal for the future European Competitiveness Fund4 that includes a dedicated policy window on ‘Resilience and Security, Defence Industry, and Space’, encompassing activities in support of defence innovation.

This would ensure the AGILE-type actions can be supported and potentially scaled up, provided this framework is endorsed by co-legislators, who are currently negotiating the text. The lessons learnt from AGILE will be considered through the above-mentioned implementation, reporting and broader policy preparation work.

This will allow the Commission to identify the most effective mechanisms to support defence innovation, informing the implementation of EU defence instruments, including the European Defence Fund5 and the EU Defence Innovation Scheme6, and the design and implementation of possible successor programmes.
